old:
Whenever we're doing Flaw and see that the argument has a Rebuttal structure, we want to be sensitive to a few common flaws relating to Rebuttals
  1. Ad Hominem (dismisses a view by saying the source has a biased interest or a conflicting past)
  2. Unproven vs. Proven True (shows that someone failed to prove X but then erroneously concludes from that that X is false)
  3. Straw Man / Irrelevant Response (the rebuttal doesn't seem to have anything to do with falsifying the original position)
  This feels like #3. Why is the author thinking that it's relevant to object by saying, "Success requires a lot of hard work"? Was the popular book saying that "success doesn't require a lot of hard work"? Not as far as we've heard. So in that sense, this author is responding to a position that his opponent doesn't hold (Straw Man) or is rebutting with something irrelevant. When we're doing Flaw and we see conditional logic wording, we know to look out for the #1 famous Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw, in which the author presents a conditional logic relationship and then interprets it in some illegal reversed or negated fashion. We have a couple conditional logic indicator words here: without exception / requires
  The book says:
  successful in business → benefited from luck
  The author's rebuttal is saying:
  successful in business → lots of hard work
  Those don't conflict, of course. Success in business may require luck AND require lots of hard work.

old: I'm gonna level with you right away. This is maybe Top 3 of my least favorite problems. I think it's hot garbage from top to bottom. So take this explanation as, "Here's how LSAC might try to explain this", but it does not represent me condoning it. Based on the paragraph I would have been thinking, "Given that these species have coloration that wouldn't provide camouflage, how have they endured for a long time?" And so I would be looking for an answer that explained how they could survive for a long time, given that they have generally ineffective camouflage and few or no other adaptations. But apparently LSAC wanted us to be thinking, "Given that the black-and-white coloration seems unlikely to provide camouflage, how is it that in reality it is providing camouflage?"
new: Based on the paragraph, it's natural to think, "Given that these species have coloration that wouldn't provide camouflage, how have they endured for a long time?" And so we might look for an answer that explained how they could survive for a long time, given that they have generally ineffective camouflage and few or no other adaptations. But notice the exact wording: the coloration only "seems unlikely" to provide effective camouflage. Seems unlikely to whom? That opens a second way to resolve the paradox: "Given that the black-and-white coloration seems unlikely to provide camouflage, how is it that in reality it is providing camouflage?"
why: Removes the author's disowning of the question ('hot garbage', 'does not represent me condoning it') and replaces it with the textual cue ('seems unlikely') that points to the credited resolution.

old:
This answer is supposed to be communicating, "these black and white species really DO have effective camouflage! Even though their coloration seems (to human perception) to be unlikely to provide effective camouflage, to many animals species, their perception of color and pattern might be such that to them this black and white coloration is effective camouflage."

Where do I begin with my problems with this answer choice?
- when I read in an LSAT paragraph that these species have coloration that seems unlikely to provide effective camouflage, I am assuming that this is a FACT coming from a source that is informed about the animal kingdom, not an uninformed opinion by someone who just looks at black and white and says "I reckon that wouldn't be good camouflage".

- it seems like a high percentage of us (maybe even a majority) already know what (C) is saying. It doesn't provide any new information, because it is already thoroughly within normal common sense that there are differences in how animals of different species perceive color and pattern.

- the intended logical force of this answer is only very weakly suggested by the actual language of the answer. There's a big gap between "many animals perceive color/pattern differently from how humans do" and "these animals find this black and white coloration difficult to discern".

My recommendation for all of us is to ignore this question ever existed. There is nothing to learn here except the humility that comes with knowing that the test writers sometimes just write terrible questions that we can't blame ourselves for not finding our way through.
new:
This answer is communicating, "these black and white species really DO have effective camouflage! Even though their coloration seems (to human perception) to be unlikely to provide effective camouflage, to many animal species, their perception of color and pattern might be such that to them this black and white coloration is effective camouflage."

The paradox only works if the coloration really fails as camouflage. But the stimulus never says it fails. It says the coloration "seems unlikely" to work, and that judgment comes from how the coloration looks to us.

If many predators do not perceive color or pattern the way humans do, then a pattern that looks conspicuous to us may be hard for those predators to pick out. That would explain how prey with few other defenses have endured for a long time.

(C) doesn't prove that this particular coloration works against these particular predators, but it gives us a plausible way for the coloration to protect the prey, and that is all a resolve answer needs to do. The lesson: when a paradox rests on how something "seems", look for an answer that separates appearance from reality.
why: The correct-answer note argued against the key and told students to ignore the question; the new note explains why C resolves the discrepancy, tied to 'seems unlikely' and C's wording about predator perception.
evidence: C: 'Animals of many predatory species do not perceive color or pattern in the same manner as humans do.' Stimulus: 'seems unlikely to provide effective camouflage.'

old:
After reading the argument on a Parallel question, we have to decide whether we think it would be more effective to make an Algebra Recipe for the argument or to just boil it down to a Principle or Reasoning Pattern. My general rule of thumb is that if there's conditional logic or quantifiers or Overlapping Ideas, then I'll go for Algebra. The first two premises are quantified/conditional logic (no / every). And there are Overlapping Ideas: Carriage Books, nonfiction book, profit, publish are all mentioned at least twice. So if we assign them some variables, we can look at the logic.
```
Premise 1 — No X's from Thing A have ever been Y.
  For Thing A (all time): if X → no Y
Premise 2 — Every Z from Thing A's last year was Y.
```
